title: Codominance & multiple alleles
examples: How does the blood type determine the alleles?
Can you explain the difference between codominance and incomplete dominance?
What happens when two different alleles are present at the same time?

explain.say: Today we are learning about how genes can show different patterns.

items: We look at blood types today.
We will see incomplete dominance too.

explain.say: First we look at the ABO blood group system in humans.
In codominance both alleles are fully expressed on the phenotype.
For example blood type AB shows both A and B antigens clearly.

draw.text: AB blood type: A and B

explain.say: Next we study incomplete dominance where the trait is blended.
For instance a red flower crossed with a white flower makes pink offspring.

faq.q: What is the difference between codominance and incomplete dominance?
faq.a: In codominance, both traits appear separately, like in blood type AB. In incomplete dominance, the two traits blend together to make a new intermediate appearance.
asks: How do I tell them apart?

faq.q: Does having two different alleles mean the trait is blended?
faq.a: Not always. If the alleles are codominant, both traits will show up distinctly, not blended.
asks: What if both genes are visible?

faq.q: Why is the ABO blood group a good example of codominance?
faq.a: Because the A and B antigens are both physically present on the red blood cells at the same time, showing both genes' effects.
asks: Why can't I have both A and B types?

faq.q: If I have one red allele and one white allele, what color will I be?
faq.a: You will show the blended color, which is pink, because the genes are exhibiting incomplete dominance.
asks: What is the result of mixing red and white?
Is the result always a mix?

faq.q: Are these patterns only seen in blood types?
faq.a: No, these genetic patterns can be observed in many different traits, like flower color in some plants.
asks: Can this happen in other organisms?
Is this limited to human blood?

facts: Codominance means both alleles are expressed simultaneously.
Incomplete dominance results in a blended phenotype.
The ABO system involves multiple alleles: A, B, and O.
Type AB blood displays both A and B antigens.

quiz.say: If an organism has alleles for yellow and red fur, and the result is orange fur, this pattern is:
quiz.why: The blending of two distinct traits to create a new intermediate trait is the definition of incomplete dominance.

wrong.1: This is wrong because codominance means both yellow and red would appear separately, not blended into orange.
wrong.2: This is wrong because simple dominance suggests one trait would completely hide the other, which did not happen here.
wrong.3: This is wrong because recessive expression implies one trait is hidden entirely, which is not the case with a visible blend.

quiz.say: In the ABO system, what blood type has both A and B antigens present?
quiz.why: Type AB blood is the classic example of codominance because both A and B antigens are fully expressed.

wrong.0: This is wrong because Type O has neither the A nor the B antigen present.
wrong.2: This is wrong because Type A only expresses the A antigen, not both A and B.
wrong.3: This is wrong because Type B only expresses the B antigen, not both A and B.

quiz.say: If a parent with the allele for purple flowers crosses with a parent with the allele for white flowers, and the offspring are pink, what pattern is shown?
quiz.why: The resulting pink color is a blend, indicating that the two alleles are interacting by blending their physical traits.

wrong.1: This is wrong because codominance would mean you see distinct purple patches and white patches, not a uniform pink.
wrong.2: This is wrong because complete dominance would mean only one color, like purple, would be visible.
wrong.3: This is wrong because while multiple alleles exist, the interaction described (blending) defines incomplete dominance.
